extensions: Implement a milestone event bus (internal pub/sub or webhook-style queue) that milestone-firing code publishes to, rather than calling the social post function directly. This decouples the milestone detection logic from the delivery logic and allows future channels (email, push, Slack) to subscribe to the same events without touching milestone code.

Add per-platform rate-limit tracking with a Redis TTL counter per user per platform. Twitter/X enforces 17 posts per 15 minutes per user token; LinkedIn rate-limits OAuth app writes at the app level. Without this, a user who hits three milestones in rapid succession will produce silent failures on the third post.

Expose a milestone-post configuration schema (stored per-app, overridable per-user) that defines which milestones trigger posts, what template each uses, and which platforms are included — enabling a future 'manage your auto-posts' screen without requiring a migration.
nonObviousAngles: OAuth token scope granted at connection time must include write permissions for each platform — but most apps request read-only or minimal scopes at signup to reduce drop-off. If users connected their accounts before this feature existed (under a read-only scope), retroactively posting on their behalf is impossible without a re-auth flow that the idea does not account for.

Posting without confirmation is a known GDPR and platform-ToS risk surface. Twitter/X and LinkedIn explicitly prohibit automating posts 'without meaningful user control' in their developer agreements; a violation can result in app-level suspension — not just individual user token revocation — taking down the integration for all users simultaneously.

weaknesses.text: Single upfront OAuth consent does not constitute legally valid ongoing consent for automated public posts under GDPR Article 7, CCPA, and most platform developer policies. A user who grants OAuth write permission to 'connect their account' has not meaningfully consented to the app posting on their behalf every time they hit an internal milestone. LinkedIn and Meta treat automated posting without per-post or per-milestone class consent as a violation, and have suspended apps for this exact pattern. GDPR fines for unlawful processing start at 2% of global annual turnover.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: LinkedIn's Marketing API and Meta's Pages API both require app review by the platform before write operations work in production (not just sandbox). LinkedIn's app review process currently takes 4–8 weeks and is frequently rejected for apps that cannot demonstrate enterprise-grade use cases. If either review is not already approved, this feature cannot ship to users on those platforms, and the event bus, rate-limit tracking, and configuration schema are all sunk cost.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: There is no rollback or retraction mechanism for a post that fires incorrectly — a bug in milestone detection logic, a misconfigured template, or a duplicate event on the pub/sub bus could post garbled, offensive, or repeated content to every connected user's public social profiles simultaneously. Social media posts are publicly visible within seconds and indexed by search engines within minutes. A single bad deploy causing mass erroneous posts is an irreversible brand and legal event, not a recoverable bug.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: Platform rate limits are also per-app (developer account level), not just per-user. If 10,000 users each hit a milestone within a short window (after a product launch or gamification event), the per-user Redis counters will all be under limit while the app-level API limit is saturated. Posts will fail silently or with transient errors, with no user-visible feedback.
weaknesses.label: resolvable

weaknesses.text: OAuth access tokens expire, and refresh tokens can be revoked by the user at the platform level without any webhook notification to the consuming app. The event bus will happily enqueue milestone posts for users whose tokens have been silently revoked, generating 401s with no user notification that their posts are not being delivered.
weaknesses.label: resolvable

risks: A milestone detection bug or template misconfiguration during a high-traffic period fires erroneous or embarrassing posts to thousands of users' public social profiles simultaneously — not recoverable and will generate support volume, press coverage, and potential legal action within hours.

LinkedIn or Meta's automated policy enforcement flags the app's developer account and suspends write API access, taking down the feature for all users with no advance warning and a multi-week reinstatement process.

A user posts about a milestone they consider private (a financial goal, a health metric, a recovery milestone) because the milestone-to-post mapping was configured without their awareness of which milestones trigger posts — resulting in public disclosure they did not intend, creating personal harm and a GDPR Article 17 complaint.
The pub/sub event bus delivers milestone events out of order or duplicates them during a broker restart, resulting in users receiving the same milestone post multiple times on the same platform.
failureModes: A user who connected their social account months ago and forgot about the integration now has the app auto-posting to their LinkedIn — visible to their employer who had no idea they used the app. The user files a GDPR complaint. The single-consent-at-OAuth-connection model has no defence in this scenario.

The milestone event bus experiences a delivery backlog and clears a queue of 50,000 held milestone events the moment it recovers — flooding all connected platforms in a burst, saturating the app-level API quota, and posting outdated milestones from weeks ago as if they just occurred.

A template variable is missing for a new milestone type, resulting in posts reading 'I just achieved null on [App Name]!' being sent to users' public profiles before the bug is caught, with no kill switch to halt delivery mid-queue.

userChallenges: Users do not read OAuth permission screens — they click 'Allow' to get past the gate, not to grant informed consent to automated future posts. When a post fires unexpectedly, the user's experience is not 'I consented to this' — it is 'the app posted without asking me.'

Milestone moments are often private or contextually inappropriate for public posting. A user who hits a '100 days sober' milestone on a wellness app, or a financial savings target, may be deeply uncomfortable having that broadcast to their LinkedIn automatically. The developer defines which milestones trigger posts, but the developer does not know which milestones are sensitive for which users.

The per-user configuration schema adds a settings surface that users will not find. Users do not navigate to settings to disable features they do not know exist — they discover the feature only when a post fires unexpectedly, at which point they are already embarrassed or angry.

The per-platform rate-limit tracking handles the platform's rate limits but does nothing about the user's own social media posting rhythm. A user who manually posts carefully curated content twice a week to LinkedIn will have that feed interrupted by app-generated milestone posts they did not choose to share.
adoptionRisks: The first unwanted auto-post is a permanent trust breakage event. An embarrassing post to a user's LinkedIn is irreversible — it has already been seen before they can delete it. Users who experience this revoke access immediately and leave a one-star review. Adoption is a one-shot event: the feature either works perfectly the first time, or it loses that user permanently.

Users already have a workaround for sharing milestones: they do it themselves, on their own schedule, with their own words. Manual sharing is not a pain point users are asking to have automated — it is a moment of personal expression and timing judgement that users actively value. This feature is optimised for the developer's virality metric, not the user's sharing experience.

Disconnecting a social account is the predictable user response to any unwanted auto-post — which directly destroys the feature's stated purpose. If the first unexpected post causes the user to revoke OAuth access, the feature has negative expected value: it loses future legitimate sharing opportunities in exchange for one uncontrolled post.

The feature is not self-discoverable as a benefit — it is only discoverable as a negative surprise. When the first post fires, the user's discovery experience is a notification from LinkedIn or Twitter saying something was posted, not an in-app moment of delight. Discovery-via-surprise is adoption-hostile.

strengths: The milestone event bus is a composable primitive that can power consent-gated share flows, referral campaigns, and manual share CTAs — the underlying infrastructure has value even if the auto-post design is rejected.
The configuration schema enabling per-user milestone-to-platform mapping is the right data model for any social sharing feature, including a properly consent-gated version.
The per-platform rate-limit tracking correctly identifies a real operational need that any social posting feature requires.
suggestedPivots: Add a lightweight confirmation step — a single-tap 'Share this milestone?' notification with a 60-second window before posting — satisfying LinkedIn's and Meta's human-in-the-loop requirement while preserving low-friction sharing.
Obtain explicit granular consent at the point of enabling auto-posting (not folded into the initial OAuth grant), recording consent timestamp and text version server-side to satisfy GDPR Article 7.
Implement a minimum 60-second post-hold queue between milestone detection and API delivery, enabling a kill-switch to drain the queue on bad-deploy detection before posts reach user profiles.
openQuestions: Has LinkedIn Partner Programme approval and Meta App Review been applied for, and what is the expected timeline? These are hard blockers that cannot be parallelised with the build.
Does the existing milestone system guarantee exactly-once delivery, or does it use at-least-once semantics that require idempotent consumers at every downstream step?

What is the actual share-to-post conversion rate when users are shown a preview step versus no preview — is there evidence that removing confirmation increases net shares, or does it increase posts-sent while decreasing user satisfaction?
